topics.title: Number systems (Binary and Decimal)
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Number systems (Binary and Decimal).

pages.title: Digits
pages.content:
How do you read a number, say $32510$? \
How big is this number exactly? \
Value of $32510$ is equivalent to $30000+2000+500+10+0$  
which can be simplified as $3 \cdot 10^4 + 2 \cdot 10^3 + 5 \cdot 10^2 + 1 \cdot 10^1 + 0 \cdot 10^0$

This is the value of $32510$ in the decimal number system, where we use $10$ numbers are used as digits. \
$0, 1, 2, ..., 9$ are use to represent one single digit. 

Can we use more or less digits than $10$? \
Yes, in fact all the computers work on a number system with only $2$ digits.

pages.title: Bits
pages.content:
The binary number system uses $2$ digits - or $0$, $1$ bits. \
Whereas, the decimal number system uses $10$ digits.

Say, we have a number in binary number system - $1001110$. \
What is the value of this number?

$10011101 = 1 \cdot 2^7 + 0 \cdot 2^6 + 0 \cdot 2^5 + 1 \cdot 2^4 + 1 \cdot 2^3 + 1 \cdot 2^2 + 0 \cdot 2^1 + 1 \cdot 2^0$ \
$10011101 = 157$ in decimal number system.

Note that in all the number systems, a number with more digits is always greater than the one with less digits (after removing leading zeroes).

So, $111...1$ ($x$ digits) is always smaller than $100...0$ ($y$ digits) if $x < y$.

The leftmost bit is called the Most Significant Bit or MSB. \
The rightmost bit is called the Least Significant Bit or LSB. \
This is because of the value they carry in the number.

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Bits and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

For example $..1101 \ 00...00$

options: The number is an odd integer
The number is a prime number
checkpoint.explanation: Each trailing zero represents a factor of 2. An integer with x trailing zeros in binary is an exact multiple of 2^x.

pages.title: MCQ - Convert to Binary
pages.content:
To convert a number from decimal to binary:
- check the remainder of the number when divided by 2, and add it to front of the binary number
- divide the number by 2
- repeat until the number is 0

Using these steps, let's convert 203 to binary.
- remainder is 1. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 1.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 101.
- remainder is 1. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 11.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 50.
- remainder is 0. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 25.
- remainder is 1. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 1011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 12.
- remainder is 0. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 01011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 6.
- remainder is 0. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 001011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 3.
- remainder is 1. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 1001011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 1.
- remainder is 1. After adding it to the front of the binary number, the binary number becomes 11001011.
- dividing the number by 2, it becomes 0.

Using these steps convert $23$ from decimal number system to binary number system.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Convert to Binary and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: Which sequence of operations converts a positive integer N into its binary representation?
options: Repeatedly taking the remainder N % 2 and dividing N = N / 2 until N = 0
Taking the square root of N repeatedly
checkpoint.explanation: Standard radix conversion repeatedly extracts the least significant bit via N % 2 and shifts right via integer division N / 2.

pages.title: Bitwise Operators
pages.content:
Operations like additions, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, etc.\
Are defined on the values of the numbers and not on any particular number system.

Say, $a + b = c$ will always be true irrespective of which number system $a$, $b$ and $c$ are represented as.

But some operations are specifically defined in the binary number system exclusively. \
These are called Bitwise operations. We will learn more about them in the next module.

pages.content:
Evaluate the following expression - 
- $10111$ $\&$ $101101$
- $10111$ $|$ $101101$

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Bitwise AND OR and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

Assume the largest possible answer is always correct

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise AND
pages.content: What can you say about the value of $C$ $=$ $A$ $\&$ $B$ with respect to $A$, $B$?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Bitwise AND and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: For any two non-negative integers A and B, what is always true about the bitwise AND result C = A & B?
checkpoint.explanation: The bitwise AND can only keep bits that are set in BOTH A and B. It cannot set any bit that is 0 in either operand, so C can never exceed min(A, B).

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise OR
pages.content: What can you say about the value of $C$ $=$ $A | B$ with respect to $A$, $B$?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Bitwise OR and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: For any two non-negative integers A and B, what is always true about the bitwise OR result C = A | B?
checkpoint.explanation: Bitwise OR includes every bit that is set in either A or B. Hence, the resulting number is at least as large as the larger operand: C >= max(A, B).

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise XOR
pages.content: Evaluate the following expression $00010111$ ^ $00101101$, where ^ denotes XOR operator.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Bitwise XOR and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: What is the result of evaluating 00010111 ^ 00101101 in binary?
checkpoint.explanation: Bitwise XOR yields 1 where bits differ and 0 where bits match: 00010111 ^ 00101101 = 00111010 (32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 58).

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise XOR Again
pages.content: What can you say about the value of $C$ $=$ $A$ `^` $B$ with respect to $A$, $B$?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Bitwise XOR Again and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: What is the result of evaluating X ^ X for any integer X?
checkpoint.explanation: Every bit in X is identical to the corresponding bit in X. Since 1 ^ 1 = 0 and 0 ^ 0 = 0, XORing any integer with itself always results in 0.

pages.title: MCQ - OR Operation with 1 Less
pages.content: What will be the value of $N$ $|$ $(N - 1)$, if $N$ is odd?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - OR Operation with 1 Less and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: If N is an odd integer, what is the value of N | (N - 1)?
checkpoint.explanation: If N is odd, its least significant bit is 1. N - 1 is identical to N except its LSB is 0. Performing bitwise OR keeps the LSB as 1, so N | (N - 1) = N.

pages.title: MCQ - XOR Operation With 1 Less
pages.content: What will be the value of $N$ ^ $(N - 1)$ if $N$ is odd?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - XOR Operation With 1 Less and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: If N is an odd integer, what is the value of N ^ (N - 1)?
checkpoint.explanation: For odd N, N and N - 1 differ ONLY at the least significant bit (bit 0). All higher bits match and cancel to 0 under XOR, leaving exactly 1.

pages.title: MCQ - Left Shift on 1
pages.content:
### Left Shift by B Bits: Binary Mechanics

Bitwise left-shift (`A << B`) shifts all binary digits of $A$ to the left by $B$ positions, appending $B$ zeros on the right.

For $1 \ll B$:
- $1 \ll 0 = 0001_2 = 1 = 2^0$
- $1 \ll 1 = 0010_2 = 2 = 2^1$
- $1 \ll 2 = 0100_2 = 4 = 2^2$
- $1 \ll B = 2^B$

This provides an $O(1)$ CPU-native way to compute powers of 2.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Left Shift on 1 and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: What mathematical expression is bitwise left-shift (1 << B) equivalent to for non-negative B?
checkpoint.explanation: Shifting the binary number 1 to the left by B positions places a 1 at position B with zeros elsewhere, which represents 2^B.

pages.title: MCQ - Right Shift Operation
pages.content:
What is $A >> B$ equivalent to?

(^ denotes power here)

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Right Shift Operation and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: What mathematical operation is bitwise right-shift (A >> B) equivalent to for non-negative integers?
checkpoint.explanation: Each single right shift divides the number by 2 and discards the remainder. Shifting right by B positions is equivalent to integer division by 2^B.

steps.title: Check prerequisites
steps.goal: Binary/decimal representation and integer arithmetic.
steps.action: Recall the prerequisite idea and answer one tiny self-check before moving on.
steps.exitCriteria: I can explain the prerequisite without opening another lesson.

steps.title: Build the mental model
steps.goal: Bitwise operations manipulate individual binary digits and enable compact tests, masks, parity checks, and state compression.
steps.action: Read the concept explanation and identify the input, state, operation, and desired output.
steps.exitCriteria: I can describe what the technique stores/changes and why it exists.

steps.title: Learn when to use it
steps.goal: Look for powers of two, parity, subset masks, toggling, or low-level integer properties.
steps.action: Classify two short problem statements and name the pattern before looking at solutions.
steps.exitCriteria: I can give at least two signals that this technique applies.

steps.title: Trace a tiny example
steps.goal: Write operands in binary and apply AND/OR/XOR/shift one bit at a time.
steps.action: Simulate the algorithm on paper, recording the invariant/state after each step.
steps.exitCriteria: I can predict the final state/output for a small example.

steps.title: Implement with scaffolding
steps.goal: State the bit property -> construct the mask/expression -> test on a tiny binary example -> generalize.
steps.action: Write pseudocode from the invariant, then translate one step at a time into C++.
steps.exitCriteria: The guided implementation works on the basic example and one edge case.

steps.title: Solve a small variation
steps.goal: Predict the result of a few bit expressions before using a compiler.
steps.action: Solve a tiny variation without copying the worked example.
steps.exitCriteria: I can adapt the approach to a changed input or requirement.

steps.title: Climb the problem ladder
steps.goal: Start with the easiest related problem and move toward mixed/harder problems only after explaining the previous solution.
steps.action: Use the practice set in increasing difficulty. Record pattern, invariant, complexity, and failed attempts.
steps.exitCriteria: I can solve a fresh problem and explain why the chosen approach is correct.

steps.title: Pass the mastery gate
steps.goal: Explain the binary invariant behind the trick instead of memorizing the expression.
steps.action: Complete the mastery checklist and one unseen variation under a reasonable time limit.
steps.exitCriteria: Mastery achieved when I can explain the binary invariant behind the trick instead of memorizing the expression.

pages.title: MCQ - OR of Array
pages.content: If we perform OR operation on all the elements of an array and store it in a variable **Array_Or**. Formally, **Array_Or** =  $A_0 | A_1 | A_2 | ....| A_n$ , what can be said about the bits in **Array_Or**?

callout.title: Key takeaway

checkpoint.question: Which principle is most important when working with MCQ - OR of Array?

Assume the largest possible answer is always correct

pages.title: MCQ - XOR of Two Numbers
pages.content: If we have two variables $A$ and $B$. All the set bits in $B$ are also set in $A$. Formally ${A} \& {B} = {B}$. Then what can we say about $C$ = $A \oplus B$, where $\oplus$ is XOR operator.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - XOR of Two Numbers and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: If all set bits in B are also set in A (i.e., A & B == B), what does A ^ B evaluate to?
options: A - B (clearing B’s set bits from A)
checkpoint.explanation: When B is a subset of A’s set bits, XORing flips those specific 1s to 0 without introducing any borrows, which is mathematically identical to A - B.

pages.title: Weapon Value

callout.title: Key takeaway

pages.title: MCQ - Which Bitwise Operator
pages.content:
A competition with $N$ participants (numbered $1$ through $N$) is taking place in Chefland. There are ${N−1}$ rounds in the competition; in each round, two arbitrarily chosen contestants battle, one of them loses and drops out of the competition. There are 10 types of weapons (numbered 1 through 10). You are given $N$ binary strings $1, 2, …, S $, each strings contains information about the weapons held by the contestant. If the character at an index is '1', the contestant has that type of weapon, otherwise the contestant doesn't have that weapon. During each battle, if the contestants have same type of weapon, that type of weapon is destroyed; after the battle, the winner collects all remaining (not destroyed) weapons of the loser. Note that each contestant may win or lose regardless of the weapons he/she has.

For Example: 
If the two contestant have the following strings  
0101010111  
1011011010  
the winner will have the weapons  
1110001101

Which operator do these fights resemble?

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Which Bitwise Operator and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: Which bitwise operation is best suited to determine the single non-duplicate number in an array where every other number appears twice?
options: Bitwise XOR (^), accumulating all elements into a single running value
checkpoint.explanation: Because XOR is commutative, associative, and X ^ X = 0 while X ^ 0 = X, all duplicate pairs cancel each other out, leaving only the unique element.

pages.title: MCQ - XOR Properties
pages.content:
### Mathematical Axioms of Bitwise XOR

The Bitwise XOR operator ($\oplus$) possesses four foundational mathematical properties:
1. **Identity:** $X \oplus 0 = X$
2. **Self-Inverse:** $X \oplus X = 0$
3. **Commutativity:** $A \oplus B = B \oplus A$
4. **Associativity:** $(A \oplus B) \oplus C = A \oplus (B \oplus C)$

Unlike bitwise OR, XOR is invertible: if $C = A \oplus B$, then $A = C \oplus B$.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - XOR Properties and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid mathematical property of the bitwise XOR operator?
options: A ^ B is always greater than or equal to A | B
A ^ A = 0 and A ^ 0 = A (Self-inverse and Identity)
checkpoint.explanation: XOR cancels matching 1 bits, whereas OR preserves all 1 bits. Thus A ^ B can never exceed A | B.

pages.title: MCQ - Powers of Two
pages.content: What happens when we subtract $2^N$ from a number.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Powers of Two and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: How can you check if an integer N > 0 is an exact power of two using bitwise operators?
checkpoint.explanation: A power of two has exactly one set bit (e.g., 1000_2 = 8). N - 1 flips that bit to 0 and all lower bits to 1 (0111_2 = 7). Hence N & (N - 1) == 0.

pages.title: MCQ - Minimum Operations
pages.content:
You are given an array $A$ of length $N$.

You can perform the following operation on the array any number of times:

- Choose any [subsequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsequence) $S$ of the array $A$ and a **positive** integer $X$ such that $X$ is a power of $2$ and subtract $X$ from all the elements of the subsequence $S$.

What will be the **minimum** number of operations required to make all the elements of the array equal to $0$ if the array in binary is [10010, 100011, 11, 10001]

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ - Minimum Operations and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

checkpoint.question: How do you toggle the k-th bit (0-indexed) of an integer N?
checkpoint.explanation: XORing with (1 << k) inverts the k-th bit (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0) while leaving all other bits unaffected.

topics.learningTrack: Concept → Intuition → Dry Run → Guided Build → Micro Practice → Independent Practice → Mastery

steps.title: Check prerequisites
steps.goal: Binary/decimal representation and integer arithmetic.
steps.action: Recall the prerequisite idea and answer one tiny self-check before moving on.
steps.exitCriteria: I can explain the prerequisite without opening another lesson.

steps.title: Build the mental model
steps.goal: Bitwise operations manipulate individual binary digits and enable compact tests, masks, parity checks, and state compression.
steps.action: Read the concept explanation and identify the input, state, operation, and desired output.
steps.exitCriteria: I can describe what the technique stores/changes and why it exists.

steps.title: Learn when to use it
steps.goal: Look for powers of two, parity, subset masks, toggling, or low-level integer properties.
steps.action: Classify two short problem statements and name the pattern before looking at solutions.
steps.exitCriteria: I can give at least two signals that this technique applies.

steps.title: Trace a tiny example
steps.goal: Write operands in binary and apply AND/OR/XOR/shift one bit at a time.
steps.action: Simulate the algorithm on paper, recording the invariant/state after each step.
steps.exitCriteria: I can predict the final state/output for a small example.

steps.title: Implement with scaffolding
steps.goal: State the bit property -> construct the mask/expression -> test on a tiny binary example -> generalize.
steps.action: Write pseudocode from the invariant, then translate one step at a time into C++.
steps.exitCriteria: The guided implementation works on the basic example and one edge case.

steps.title: Solve a small variation
steps.goal: Predict the result of a few bit expressions before using a compiler.
steps.action: Solve a tiny variation without copying the worked example.
steps.exitCriteria: I can adapt the approach to a changed input or requirement.

steps.title: Climb the problem ladder
steps.goal: Start with the easiest related problem and move toward mixed/harder problems only after explaining the previous solution.
steps.action: Use the practice set in increasing difficulty. Record pattern, invariant, complexity, and failed attempts.
steps.exitCriteria: I can solve a fresh problem and explain why the chosen approach is correct.

steps.title: Pass the mastery gate
steps.goal: Explain the binary invariant behind the trick instead of memorizing the expression.
steps.action: Complete the mastery checklist and one unseen variation under a reasonable time limit.
steps.exitCriteria: Mastery achieved when I can explain the binary invariant behind the trick instead of memorizing the expression.

What do the constraints allow?
What is the simplest correct approach?
What work repeats?
What invariant/state should stay true?
What edge cases break the approach?
What are the time and space costs?
